scenes.claim: Compact thought needs a dense image field.
scenes.narration: The starting problem is a mismatch: CTM keeps thought compact, while super-resolution must predict detail at many image locations. A compact state alone does not naturally carry the dense spatial evidence the reconstruction needs.

objects.text: Compact thought needs a dense image field.

scenes.claim: ThinkSR adds a dense carrier to compact thought.
scenes.narration: ThinkSR keeps a persistent dense carrier that can store spatial information through the reconstruction process. The compact thought process reads that carrier and writes updates back into it.

objects.text: ThinkSR adds a dense carrier to compact thought.

scenes.claim: The carrier starts as encoded low-resolution features.
scenes.narration: The low-resolution image is encoded into a feature field, written as F equals E of the low-resolution input. That feature field is then windowed into X, so the dense carrier can be processed in local pieces.

objects.text: The carrier starts as encoded low-resolution features.

scenes.claim: The model repeats one thought process across windows.
scenes.narration: The end-to-end path is encoder, windows, shared DQ-CTM ticks, and decoder. Sharing the ticking process lets the method update many window features without replacing the dense carrier.

objects.text: The model repeats one thought process across windows.

scenes.claim: DQ-CTM is the dense version of the CTM idea.
scenes.narration: The comparison separates plain CTM, a window-wise adaptation, and DQ-CTM. The important shift is from compact-only processing toward a version that can keep dense reconstruction state.

objects.text: DQ-CTM is the dense version of the CTM idea.

scenes.claim: Repeated ticks refine the reconstruction over time.
scenes.narration: The reconstruction sequence is shown from T equals zero through T equals four. Each tick gives the dense carrier another chance to update local image detail.

objects.text: Repeated ticks refine the reconstruction over time.

scenes.claim: Error maps show where refinement still falls short.
scenes.narration: The paper checks absolute-error maps on the same image crops. A shared colour scale makes the visual comparison about error magnitude, not about changing display settings.

objects.text: Error maps show where refinement still falls short.

scenes.claim: ThinkSR is competitive with older CNN baselines.
scenes.narration: On the five-benchmark average, DQ-CTM-SR scores twenty-eight point nine eight three. That sits slightly above CARN and IMDN, and slightly below RFDN.

objects.text: ThinkSR is competitive with older CNN baselines.

scenes.claim: The strongest lightweight transformer remains ahead.
scenes.narration: CATANet has the best average in the table, at twenty-nine point four eight two. DQ-CTM-SR is lower at twenty-eight point nine eight three, so the method is not the top lightweight result.

objects.text: The strongest lightweight transformer remains ahead.

scenes.claim: The parameter cost is moderate, not minimal.
scenes.narration: DQ-CTM-SR uses one point one two nine million parameters. It is smaller than CARN, but larger than IMDN, RFDN, and CATANet in the reported table.

objects.text: The parameter cost is moderate, not minimal.

scenes.claim: ThinkSR trades peak score for a compact-dense bridge.
scenes.narration: The contribution is the bridge between compact thought and dense image state. The result is competitive with CNN baselines, but the table still leaves a clear gap to the strongest lightweight transformer. Its cost is a moderate parameter count, so the main value is the architecture idea rather than a new best benchmark.

objects.text: ThinkSR trades peak score for a compact-dense bridge.
